question: Can a state licensing board deny me an occupational license because of a criminal conviction, and how can I challenge the denial?

negative: suspension or revocation of a license only

gold_sections.why: The general rule for every Business and Professions Code board: denial for a conviction only if substantially related and within seven years (no time limit for serious felonies, sex-registration offenses and certain financial felonies); no denial after a certificate of rehabilitation, pardon, rehabilitation showing, dismissed conviction, or arrest without conviction; limits on asking about criminal history; written denial notice with challenge, appeal and record-correction information.

Substantial-relationship criteria each board must adopt (nature and gravity, time elapsed, nature and duties of the profession) and the duty to consider rehabilitation evidence before denying; criteria posted on the board's website.
Rehabilitation criteria; boards must consider a showing of rehabilitation where the sentence was completed without a parole or probation violation, or the board's own criteria are met.

On denial the board files a statement of issues or serves a notice of denial stating the reason and the right to an APA hearing if requested in writing within 60 days; otherwise the hearing is waived; service by mail complete on mailing.

The decision or notice must state the earliest reapplication date (one year unless the board sets an earlier date or another statute a later one), that rehabilitation evidence will be considered on reapplication, and include the rehabilitation criteria.
A requested hearing must be held within 90 days unless the applicant agrees to postpone; OAH may add up to 45 days (180 in exam or licensing fraud cases), at most two such orders.
What the board may do after the hearing: grant, grant on probation (revoke, stay, probationary conditions), deny, or other action.
The record of conviction is conclusive only of the fact of conviction; same three relation criteria; no categorical bar by type of conviction without considering rehabilitation.
This division governs denials for conviction; no denial for lack of good moral character or similar character grounds.
Exclusions: the State Bar (Chapter 4, Section 6000), alcoholic beverage licenses (Division 9) and gambling control (Chapter 5 of Division 8) are outside these rules (except Section 494.5).
Separate, older-style rules for the Bureau for Private Postsecondary Education, the State Athletic Commission and the California Horse Racing Board, which 480 does not govern.
An agency may deny without a new hearing if it denied the same applicant on the same ground after an APA hearing within the previous year.
Conviction means a judgment after a guilty plea or verdict, nolo contendere plea or finding of guilt; boards may not deny an applicant otherwise qualified under 480(b) or (c).
'Board' includes bureaus, commissions, departments and agencies; 'license' includes certificates and registrations.
An APA licensing hearing starts with a statement of issues; when the applicant requested the hearing it is sent with the notice of hearing under 11509 (no notice of defense needed).
Notice of hearing at least 10 days before the hearing; rights to counsel at own expense, to present evidence, cross-examine and subpoena.
ALJ proposed decision within 30 days after submission (missing it does not prejudice the agency); the agency acts within 100 days or the proposed decision is deemed adopted.
Reconsideration on petition; the agency's power expires 30 days after delivery or mailing of the decision; petitions not acted on are deemed denied.

Judicial review by petition for writ of mandate within 30 days after the last day reconsideration can be ordered (extended if the record is requested within 10 days); reconsideration is not a prerequisite.

Administrative mandamus: the court asks whether the agency acted beyond its jurisdiction, gave a fair trial, or prejudicially abused its discretion, and either sets the decision aside or denies the writ.
How to question the accuracy or completeness of the Department of Justice record (one of the Penal Code 11122-11127 processes the denial notice must describe).

nuggets.text: A board may deny a license for a conviction only if the crime is substantially related to the qualifications, functions or duties of the profession and the conviction (or the applicant's incarceration or release from it) falls within the seven years before the application.
nuggets.quote: The applicant has been convicted of a crime within the preceding seven years from the date of application that is substantially related to the qualifications, functions, or duties of the business or profession for which the application is made

nuggets.text: The seven-year limit does not apply to serious felonies (Penal Code 1192.7) or offenses requiring sex-offender registration (and, for certain listed professions, financial felonies directly related to fiduciary duties).

nuggets.text: A license may not be denied for a conviction if the person has a certificate of rehabilitation, a pardon or clemency, or has made a showing of rehabilitation under Section 482.

nuggets.text: A board may not deny a license based on an arrest that ended in anything other than a conviction (including an infraction, citation or juvenile adjudication).
nuggets.quote: a board shall not deny a license on the basis of an arrest that resulted in a disposition other than a conviction, including an arrest that resulted in an infraction, citation, or a juvenile adjudication

nuggets.text: Whether a crime is substantially related is judged by (1) the nature and gravity of the offense, (2) the years elapsed since the offense, and (3) the nature and duties of the profession.
nuggets.quote: The nature and gravity of the offense. (2) The number of years elapsed since the date of the offense. (3) The nature and duties of the profession in which the applicant seeks licensure or in which the licensee is licensed.

nuggets.text: A board may not deny a license wholly or partly because of a conviction without considering the applicant's evidence of rehabilitation.

nuggets.text: The board must consider whether the applicant has shown rehabilitation if the applicant completed the sentence without a parole or probation violation (or meets the board's rehabilitation criteria).
nuggets.quote: Each board shall consider whether an applicant or licensee has made a showing of rehabilitation if either of the following are met: (1) The applicant or licensee has completed the criminal sentence at issue without a violation of parole or probation.

nuggets.text: The board must hold a requested hearing within 90 days of the request unless the applicant asks for or agrees in writing to a postponement.
nuggets.quote: the board shall conduct such hearing within 90 days from the date the hearing is requested unless the applicant shall request or agree in writing to a postponement or continuance of the hearing

nuggets.text: After the hearing the board may grant the license, grant it on probation (revoked, revocation stayed, probationary conditions), or deny it.
nuggets.quote: Grant the license effective upon completion of all licensing requirements by the applicant, immediately revoke the license, stay the revocation, and impose probationary conditions on the license, which may include suspension. (3) Deny the license.

nuggets.text: The agency may reconsider its decision on a party's petition, but its power to do so expires 30 days after the decision is delivered or mailed.
nuggets.quote: The power to order a reconsideration shall expire 30 days after the delivery or mailing of a decision to a respondent

nuggets.text: Court review is by petition for a writ of mandate under the Code of Civil Procedure, filed within 30 days after the last day on which reconsideration can be ordered.
nuggets.quote: Judicial review may be had by filing a petition for a writ of mandate in accordance with the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, subject, however, to the statutes relating to the particular agency. Except as otherwise provided in this section, the petition shall be filed within 30 days after the last day on which reconsideration can be ordered.

nuggets.text: The decision or denial notice must state the earliest date to reapply, which is one year from the decision's effective date or service of the notice unless the board sets an earlier date or another statute a later one.
nuggets.quote: The earliest date on which the applicant may reapply for a license which shall be one year from the effective date of the decision, or service of the notice under subdivision (b) of Section 485, unless the board prescribes an earlier date or a later date is prescribed by another statute.

answer:
Yes, but only in limited cases. Boards under California's Business and Professions Code may deny a license for a conviction only if the crime is substantially related to the profession and you were convicted, or released from incarceration, within seven years before applying [N1]; that time limit does not cover serious felonies or sex-registration offenses [N2]. A board cannot deny you for a conviction dismissed under Penal Code 1203.4 or similar relief [N4], for an arrest that did not end in conviction [N5], or if you have a certificate of rehabilitation, a pardon, or have shown rehabilitation [N3]. Relatedness turns on the offense's nature and gravity, the years since it, and the profession's duties [N6], and the board must consider your rehabilitation evidence before denying [N7]; finishing your sentence without a parole or probation violation counts [N8].

If denied, the board must tell you in writing how to challenge or appeal and how to get and correct your record [N9]. Request a hearing in writing within 60 days after the denial notice is served, or you lose that right [N10]. The hearing must be held within 90 days unless you agree to a delay [N11]. The board may then grant the license, grant it on probation, or deny it [N12]. You can petition for reconsideration before the board's power ends 30 days after the decision is delivered [N13], and seek court review by writ of mandate within 30 days after that [N14]. You may usually reapply after one year [N15].

gaps: Section 485 lets the board either serve a notice of denial (b) or file and serve a statement of issues (a). Only the notice path, which carries the 60-day hearing request, is modelled; on the statement-of-issues path Gov. Code 11505-11506 would give 15 days to file a notice of defense.

The may_deny table covers only conviction grounds under 480(a)(1), (b), (c) and (d). Formal discipline by another board (480(a)(2)), knowingly false application statements (480(e)) and practice-act provisions that apply 'notwithstanding Section 480' are not modelled. A true denial_permitted means the board may deny, not that it must.
The 90-day hearing limit in 487 states no consequence, so it is not modelled as a timer; OAH may add up to 45 days (180 for examination or licensing fraud), no more than two orders.

Under Gov. Code 11517(c)(2) the agency has 100 days to act on the proposed decision or it is deemed adopted; this is not modelled as a timer. The decision takes effect 30 days after delivery unless reconsideration is ordered (11519).

Reconsideration is optional (11523: the right to petition is not affected by failure to seek it); the result of a granted reconsideration is not modelled. The 30-day writ deadline is extended to 30 days after delivery of the record if it is requested within 10 days after the last day reconsideration can be ordered.
The court review outcome variable set_aside is the court's judgment under CCP 1094.5(f); the standard of review (independent judgment or substantial evidence) comes from case law, not the statute.

notes: Applies to boards under the Business and Professions Code (480, as defined by 22, 23.7 and 477). Not covered: the State Bar, alcoholic beverage licenses and gambling control (476); the Bureau for Private Postsecondary Education, State Athletic Commission and Horse Racing Board, which use 480.2 instead; licenses issued under other codes (for example Health and Safety Code facility licenses, Insurance Code and Financial Code licenses, and Education Code credentials) have their own provisions; several practice acts contain provisions that operate 'notwithstanding Section 480' (for example pharmacy, 4202.6). California has no general statute for a preliminary determination before applying. Boards also may not deny for lack of good moral character (475(c)), may not categorically bar by conviction type without considering rehabilitation (493(b)(2)), generally may not require applicants to disclose criminal history (480(f)(2), except listed boards), and may deny without a new hearing an application refused on the same ground after a hearing within the past year (489). Sections 7.5, 481, 482, 488 and 493 have been operative since July 1, 2020; no pending or expired versions were found in the downloaded text. Service of the notice of denial by mail is complete on mailing (485).
